axis.star_quality.label: Star quality
axis.star_quality.beginner: How sharp and round the stars look. Big, fat, or stretched stars hurt this score.
axis.star_quality.intermediate: A composite score across star sharpness (FWHM), roundness (eccentricity), and how consistent those are across the frame. Soft or elongated stars drag it down.
axis.star_quality.advanced: Composite of median FWHM, median eccentricity, and the corner-vs-center FWHM excess. Diagnoses focus, seeing, tracking, and optical-train integrity (coma, tilt, field curvature).

axis.noise_management.label: Noise management
axis.noise_management.beginner: Whether the dark sky around your target looks clean and natural, or grainy, plasticky, or smeared.
axis.noise_management.intermediate: Combines the noise floor with the noise's spectral shape and pixel-to-pixel correlation. Aggressive noise reduction shows up here.
axis.noise_management.advanced: Noise floor (per-channel σ on background patches) + PSD shape (high-band suppression as the NR fingerprint) + autocorrelation width (drizzle/resampling smearing) + target-region SNR.

axis.detail_resolution.label: Detail resolution
axis.detail_resolution.beginner: How much real fine structure your image resolves — without faking it.
axis.detail_resolution.intermediate: Measures how power falls off with spatial frequency in the target region. Real astronomical detail follows a smooth power law; sharpening artifacts show up as bumps.
axis.detail_resolution.advanced: Radial power spectrum of the windowed target FFT. Power-law slope + the knee where power flattens into noise. Compared against the PSF-implied diffraction cutoff to flag oversharpening.

axis.gradient_control.label: Gradient control
axis.gradient_control.beginner: Whether the sky background is even, or has bright/dark patches across the frame.
axis.gradient_control.intermediate: Quantifies sky gradient (large-scale background tilt) and residual vignetting (corner darkening) — both signs of imperfect calibration or light pollution.
axis.gradient_control.advanced: Polynomial surface fit on the SEP background map (peak-to-peak in noise units) + radial-falloff fit on background-mask pixels (shell-p10 robust against bright targets).

axis.color_calibration.label: Color calibration
axis.color_calibration.beginner: Are the colors realistic and varied, or has processing crushed them all to gray?
axis.color_calibration.intermediate: Star-color diversity (matching real stellar B–V variation), background neutrality (no color cast), and per-channel balance.
axis.color_calibration.advanced: Star RGB ratio diversity vs B–V reference, background chromaticity distance from neutral, per-channel balance, plus narrowband palette detection (SHO/HOO/natural).

fwhm.label: FWHM (full width at half maximum)
fwhm.beginner: How fat your stars are, in pixels. Smaller = sharper.
fwhm.intermediate: The width of a star's brightness profile at half its peak intensity. Measured in pixels; sets a hard floor on how much detail the image can resolve.
fwhm.advanced: Full-width-at-half-maximum of the per-star fitted Moffat profile. Geometric mean of FWHM_a (major axis) and FWHM_b (minor axis). Drives the optical-system point spread function characterization.

eccentricity.label: Eccentricity
eccentricity.beginner: How stretched (vs round) your stars are. 0 = perfectly round, near 1 = very streaky.
eccentricity.intermediate: Per-star ratio of the minor axis to the major axis, expressed as sqrt(1 − (b/a)²). Patterns across the frame diagnose tracking vs. optics.
eccentricity.advanced: From the Moffat fit's (a, b) parameters: ecc = sqrt(1 − (b/a)²). Field-wide patterns analyzed via double-angle weighted mean resultant length R + radial alignment score against the field center.

psd.label: Power spectral density (PSD)
psd.beginner: A graph showing how 'busy' your image is at small vs large scales. Used to fingerprint processing.
psd.intermediate: A frequency-domain decomposition: how much power exists at each spatial scale. Different processing steps (NR, sharpening) leave characteristic signatures here.
psd.advanced: |FFT(image)|² azimuthally averaged into a 1D radial profile. White noise → flat. Suppressed mid/high frequencies → noise reduction. Boosted high frequencies → oversharpening.

mtf50.label: MTF50 / effective resolution
mtf50.beginner: The smallest detail your image actually preserves. Lower = sharper image.
mtf50.intermediate: The spatial frequency at which the image's modulation transfer function drops to half its peak. A standard sharpness benchmark.
mtf50.advanced: Modulation Transfer Function at 50% — the frequency where image contrast is halved from DC. Computed from the radial PSD's knee, comparable across systems.

snr.label: SNR (signal-to-noise ratio)
snr.beginner: How much real signal there is vs random noise. Higher = cleaner image.
snr.intermediate: Ratio of signal level to noise level — usually expressed in target regions, where you care about it most. More integration time is the most direct way to improve it.
snr.advanced: Per-pixel signal (background-subtracted luminance) divided by local noise (from the SEP RMS map). Reported as median + p90 over segmentation target pixels.

autocorrelation.label: Noise autocorrelation
autocorrelation.beginner: Measures how 'lumpy' the noise is. Tight grain = good. Smeared blobs = something smoothed your image too much.
autocorrelation.intermediate: How correlated each noise pixel is with its neighbors. True shot noise is uncorrelated (1-pixel wide); drizzle, resampling, or NR widens the correlation peak.
autocorrelation.advanced: FFT-based autocorrelation of background patches. Half-max half-width measured in pixels. A width >> 1 px is a direct signature of pixel-level smearing from drizzle, bicubic resampling, or wavelet NR.

gradient_ratio.label: Gradient ratio
gradient_ratio.beginner: How uneven your sky background is, scaled to your noise. >3× is noticeable, >10× is bad.
gradient_ratio.intermediate: Peak-to-peak of a low-order polynomial fit to the background, normalized by the noise floor. Flags light-pollution gradients and bad flats.
gradient_ratio.advanced: Peak-to-peak of a 2nd-order polynomial surface fitted to the SEP background map, divided by the median local RMS. The normalization makes it scale-invariant; rule of thumb 3× ≈ visible, 10× ≈ serious.

vignetting.label: Vignetting
vignetting.beginner: When the corners of your image look dimmer than the center because of optics or bad flat frames.
vignetting.intermediate: Radial brightness falloff from the center to the corners. Real residual vignetting after calibration usually means flats don't match the current optical setup.
vignetting.advanced: Radial-falloff model fitted to background-mask pixels using shell-p10 robust binning (so a bright central target isn't misread as 'center brightness'). Reports center-to-corner percentage.

psf.label: PSF (point spread function)
psf.beginner: The shape your optics turn a single point of light into. A perfect telescope would make a tiny dot; real ones spread it out a bit.
psf.intermediate: How a point source (a star) gets blurred by the atmosphere + optics + tracking + sensor sampling. Its width sets your image's resolution ceiling.
psf.advanced: The system's response to an idealized point input. Modeled per-star with a Moffat profile (better wings than Gaussian). Sets the diffraction-limited cutoff frequency (~1/FWHM_px) above which target detail can't be physically real.

vector_field.label: Eccentricity vector field
vector_field.beginner: A map showing each star as a tiny tick. The direction and length of the tick tells you how stretched the star is.
vector_field.intermediate: Each tick is a fitted star. Length encodes eccentricity, orientation encodes the major-axis position angle. Patterns across the frame diagnose the source of star elongation.
vector_field.advanced: Per-star (x, y, ecc, PA) plotted as line segments. Uniform tick orientation = uniform_drift (RA tracking PE); radial outward pattern = optical aberration (coma/tilt/field curvature); random orientation = atmospheric seeing.

position_angle.label: Position angle (PA)
position_angle.beginner: Which direction a star's stretching points — like the direction of an arrow.
position_angle.intermediate: The angle of a star's major-axis elongation, measured CCW from the +x axis. When all stars share a PA, the cause is mechanical (tracking, drift); when PAs vary radially, it's optical.
position_angle.advanced: Position angle of the fitted Moffat ellipse's major axis. Aggregated as a double-angle weighted mean (so the 0°/180° symmetry doesn't cancel) for the field-pattern classification.

tracking_error.label: Tracking error / periodic error
tracking_error.beginner: When the mount can't keep your scope perfectly pointed, stars trail in one direction.
tracking_error.intermediate: The mount's mechanical error in following the sky's rotation. Repetitive deviations are 'periodic error'; visible as stars elongated in one consistent direction across the whole frame.
tracking_error.advanced: Sub-arcsecond mechanical periodicity in the worm/spur gear (or strain-wave equivalent) of an EQ mount. Manifests as a uniform_drift eccentricity pattern in the field. Mitigation: PEC, autoguiding with adequate cadence, or strain-wave mounts.

optical_aberration.label: Optical aberration
optical_aberration.beginner: When the lens/mirror can't focus light cleanly, stars look distorted — usually worse at the corners.
optical_aberration.intermediate: Imperfect optics that distort star shapes systematically. The most common ones for astrophotography are coma (radial smear) and field curvature (corner softness).
optical_aberration.advanced: Off-axis aberrations (coma, astigmatism, field curvature, sensor tilt) that produce elongation oriented radially with respect to the optical axis. Show up in the ecc field as a radial pattern with concentration > 0.4.

random_seeing.label: Random seeing
random_seeing.beginner: When the air above your scope is turbulent, it stretches stars in random directions — not your scope's fault.
random_seeing.intermediate: Atmospheric turbulence on the night you imaged. Affects FWHM and eccentricity but with no consistent direction across the frame.
random_seeing.advanced: Random-direction eccentricity pattern (low double-angle mean resultant length R, low radial-alignment score). Atmosphere-driven, not equipment. Lever: subframe weighting / culling, not autoguiding.

coma.label: Coma
coma.beginner: An optical defect that makes stars near the edges of your image look like little comets pointing outward.
coma.intermediate: An off-axis aberration where stars elongate radially outward from the field center, especially in fast Newtonians without a coma corrector.
coma.advanced: Off-axis third-order aberration producing radial PA elongation that grows with field angle. Mitigation: coma corrector matched to focal ratio + image circle.

moffat.label: Moffat profile
moffat.beginner: A math curve we fit to each star to measure its size. Better at modeling real stars than the simpler 'bell curve'.
moffat.intermediate: A 2D model commonly used to describe star light profiles in real imaging. Fits both the bright core and the faint wings better than a Gaussian.
moffat.advanced: f(r) = amp · (1 + (r/α)²)^(−β) · 2D anisotropic with a constant floor. β governs wing steepness; FWHM = 2α·sqrt(2^(1/β) − 1). Preferred over Gaussian for non-diffraction-limited PSFs.

azimuthal_average.label: Azimuthally averaged
azimuthal_average.beginner: Means we averaged the same distance from the center in all directions to make a 1D graph from a 2D image.
azimuthal_average.intermediate: Collapsing a 2D quantity (like a PSD) into a 1D radial profile by averaging all points the same distance from the center.
azimuthal_average.advanced: Radial binning + per-bin mean of a 2D field, typically applied to |FFT|² to yield the radial power spectrum. Loses anisotropic information but enables 1D power-law fitting.

color_magnitude_diagram.label: Color–magnitude diagram (CMD)
color_magnitude_diagram.beginner: A scatter plot of stars where position tells you each star's color and brightness. Used to check that color survived processing.
color_magnitude_diagram.intermediate: Each dot is a star, plotted by its color index (B−V proxy) vs apparent magnitude. A healthy spread along the main sequence indicates good color preservation.
color_magnitude_diagram.advanced: Stellar color-magnitude diagram built from per-star RGB ratios (log10(R/B) as a B−V proxy) and instrumental magnitudes (−2.5·log10(total flux)). Color collapse to a vertical line indicates color information was crushed.

bv_index.label: B–V color index
bv_index.beginner: A number that tells you a star's color — small and negative for blue stars, large and positive for red stars.
bv_index.intermediate: A star's brightness in the blue filter minus its brightness in the visual filter — astronomy's standard color label, ranging from ~ −0.3 (hot blue) to ~ +1.8 (cool red).
bv_index.advanced: Photometric color index B − V (Johnson-Cousins). Correlates with stellar effective temperature; used as the photometric ground truth for evaluating star-color preservation in processed images.

percentile.label: Percentile
percentile.beginner: Your rank out of 100 compared to other images. 70 means you're better than 70 out of 100.
percentile.intermediate: Where your value falls in the distribution of reference images. Direction-corrected here, so 100 = best regardless of metric.
percentile.advanced: Direction-corrected percentile rank against the chosen APOD reference set. Always 100 = best (the pipeline inverts for lower-is-better metrics like FWHM and gradient_ratio).

p10.label: p10 / 10th percentile
p10.beginner: The value below which only 10% of the reference images fall. Useful as a 'top-tier' threshold.
p10.intermediate: 10% of the reference distribution is at or below this value. The lower-tail benchmark for distributions where lower is better.
p10.advanced: 10th percentile of the per-category reference distribution for this metric. Used in the quantile box plot as the lower whisker; outer-shell baseline for the vignetting fit also uses p10.

p50.label: p50 / median
p50.beginner: The middle value — half the reference images are above this, half below.
p50.intermediate: The median of the reference distribution. Exactly half of comparison images score better, half worse.
p50.advanced: 50th percentile (median) of the reference distribution. Robust central tendency estimator. The radar chart's 50-mark on each axis.

p90.label: p90 / 90th percentile
p90.beginner: The value below which 90% of reference images fall — a 'top 10%' threshold.
p90.intermediate: 90% of comparison images score at or below this value. Useful as the 'aspirational' end of the distribution.
p90.advanced: 90th percentile of the reference distribution. Upper whisker on quantile plots; the high-tail benchmark.

corner_fwhm_excess.label: Corner FWHM excess
corner_fwhm_excess.beginner: How much fatter your stars look at the corners of the frame compared to the center. Big number = the lens isn't sharp at the edges.
corner_fwhm_excess.intermediate: The ratio of corner-region star sharpness (median FWHM in the outer 25% of the field) to center-region sharpness (inner 50%). Large positive values indicate field curvature, sensor tilt, or coma.
corner_fwhm_excess.advanced: (median FWHM in corner annulus, r > 0.7·half-diagonal) / (median FWHM in center disk, r < 0.4·half-diagonal) − 1. Half-diagonal-based binning so it's robust across aspect ratios. Combined with the eccentricity pattern it discriminates field curvature (FWHM rises radially) from coma (eccentricity radial AND FWHM rises) from tilt (asymmetric corner-to-corner).

hf_suppression.label: High-frequency PSD suppression
hf_suppression.beginner: If your noise reduction was too heavy, the fine grain in the dark sky gets smoothed away. This number measures how much.
hf_suppression.intermediate: How much the high-frequency (small-scale) part of your background noise has been suppressed compared to its mid-frequency baseline. Big values = aggressive NR; the sky looks smooth and 'plastic' instead of having natural grain.
hf_suppression.advanced: 1 − (mean PSD power in upper band) / (mean PSD power in mid band), measured on background-only patches. >0.5 indicates aggressive low-pass NR (NoiseXTerminator on a high setting, heavy MMT/TGV). The signature is independent of overall noise level — it's the SHAPE that's diagnostic.

noise_psd_slope.label: Noise PSD spectral slope
noise_psd_slope.beginner: Tells you what the dark sky's noise 'shape' looks like. Real shot noise looks one way; over-processed noise looks another.
noise_psd_slope.intermediate: The log-log slope of the background noise's power spectrum. A flat slope (~0) means well-behaved white noise; steep negative slopes mean low-frequency lumpy noise from over-smoothing or calibration issues.
noise_psd_slope.advanced: Linear-regression slope of log(PSD) vs log(frequency) for background patches. Pure shot noise is white (slope ≈ 0). Slope < −1 indicates low-frequency dominance (NR smoothing, residual gradient). Slope > 0 indicates a high-frequency boost (oversharpening, ringing).

detail_slope.label: Target detail spectral slope
detail_slope.beginner: Real astronomical detail follows a predictable pattern. This number checks whether yours does — sharpening artifacts make it look unnatural.
detail_slope.intermediate: The log-log slope of the target region's radial power spectrum. Real diffuse astronomical structure has a smooth power-law falloff; sharpening kernels add bumps that make the slope shallower (less negative) than expected.
detail_slope.advanced: Power-law slope fit to the windowed-FFT radial power spectrum of the target region, over [0.01, 0.25] cy/px. Astronomical sources typically yield slopes in [−3, −2]. Flatter than −2 with a corresponding bump in the residual is a sharpening signature; steeper than −3 suggests over-smoothed detail.

background_sigma.label: Background σ (sigma)
background_sigma.beginner: How noisy the dark sky parts of your image are. Lower = cleaner.
background_sigma.intermediate: The standard deviation of pixel intensities in background-only regions. The fundamental noise floor of the image.
background_sigma.advanced: Sigma-clipped standard deviation of background-mask pixels per channel. The denominator in SNR; set by integration time, sensor read noise, dark current, and sky brightness.

stellar_chroma.label: Stellar chroma diversity
stellar_chroma.beginner: How much color variety your stars have — blue, white, yellow, orange — vs all looking the same.
stellar_chroma.intermediate: The spread of star colors across the detected population. Healthy images show the full stellar color sequence; over-processed ones collapse everyone to gray.
stellar_chroma.advanced: Mean inter-quartile range of normalized R/G/B ratios across detected stars. Mapped to a 0–1 score; low values flag color information destroyed by saturation, NR-on-chroma, or aggressive white balance.

background_chroma.label: Background chroma distance
background_chroma.beginner: How far your sky background is from a true neutral gray.
background_chroma.intermediate: The chromaticity distance of the median background from neutral (1/3, 1/3) in (r, g) space. Catches color casts left over from incomplete calibration.
background_chroma.advanced: Euclidean distance of the median background chromaticity from (1/3, 1/3). Independent of overall brightness; flags color casts from filters, sensors, or skipped background-neutralization steps.

channel_balance.label: Channel balance
channel_balance.beginner: Whether your red, green, and blue channels are balanced or one dominates.
channel_balance.intermediate: How far the per-channel background means deviate from each other after normalization. Big deviations indicate color calibration is off.
channel_balance.advanced: Magnitude of the (R, G, B) deviation vector from the per-channel mean, normalized by the average background level. Catches color casts and unbalanced flats.
